title: Sharper than a sword
hook: the devotees' way is unique, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair (Anand 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahsaa, and your line, the word clears. Today, pauri fourteen, and a path that's very narrow indeed.

A child walks along a curb like a balance beam. Arms out, one foot in front of the other, eyes fixed ahead, while everyone else just walks on the sidewalk. One wobble and she's off. It takes total attention, and it's strangely absorbing. Now imagine the curb gets thinner, sharp as a blade, fine as a single hair, and someone tells you this, not the wide sidewalk, is the path of those who love God. That's the fourteenth pauri of Anand Sahib.
screen: `WALKING A CURB, ARMS OUT.` → `ONE WOBBLE AND YOU'RE OFF.` → `NOW, THINNER THAN A HAIR.`

segments.voice: It opens: bhagtaa kee chaal niraalee. The way of the devotees is unique. Niraalee means distinct, set apart, one of a kind. Then, in paraphrase: they walk a hard path. They give up greed, grasping, ego and craving, and they don't talk too much. Then the famous image: khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee, et maarag jaanaa. Sharper than a double-edged sword, finer than a hair: that is the path they walk. Those who, by the Guru's grace, let go of self, their desire merges into the Lord. Says Nanak, the way of the devotees, age after age, is unique. Two details stand out. First, khanniahu, from khanda, the double-edged sword. Guru Amar Das was reaching for an everyday picture of sharpness. More than a century later, in 1699, a khanda would stir the amrit at the first Khalsa initiation, and today it stands at the center of the Sikh emblem, so Sikhs now hear this line with that blade in mind. Second, the list of what's given up: greed, grasping, ego, craving, and then, almost funny in its plainness, talking too much. Not some great austerity. Just fewer words. The path isn't hard because it's exotic. It's hard because it's narrow. Every day brings a hundred small chances to step off: a greedy thought, a proud word, one more thing to grab. The devotee's way is to stay on the line, again and again, and the ones who do, the pauri says, have let go of self by the Guru's grace.
screen: `NIRAALEE: SET APART, UNIQUE.` · `GIVE UP GREED, EGO, CRAVING.` · `AND DON'T TALK TOO MUCH.` · `SHARPER THAN A KHANDA, FINER THAN A HAIR.` · then, large: `THE NARROW WAY.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, find a line on the floor, a floorboard seam or the edge of a rug, and walk slowly along it, heel to toe, for a few steps, saying Waheguru with each one if you pray; if you can't stand, trace a line slowly with one finger. Notice the attention it takes, and how the mind goes quiet when it has one thing to do. Then sit and breathe.
Khanniahu tikhee, sharper than a double-edged sword. Vaalahu nikee, finer than a hair: the devotees' way, walked by letting go of self.
Your line: the narrow way. Even one word left unsaid is a step along it. Day three hundred ninety, done.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the khanda, the double-edged sword it names, is used to stir the amrit at the Khalsa initiation.

what it means: the devotees' way is narrow, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair, walked by letting go of greed, ego and too many words.
what a scholar hears: khanniahu is from khanda, the double-edged sword later used to prepare amrit, and vaalahu from vaal, hair: the pauri's two images measure the path from both sides.

chat.says: Why does Anand call the devotees' path sharper than a sword? Is it dangerous?
options: It's narrow: each day you can step off through greed, ego, or talking too much.
It means only a few great saints can walk it; ordinary people never could.
It's about battle: only those who fight with real swords count as devotees.
chat.meaning: Khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee: sharper than a sword, finer than a hair. It's hard because it's narrow: giving up greed, ego, craving, even extra words.
